rows.title: Berberine attenuates diabetic kidney injury via FOXO1/SP1-associated regulation of renal SGLT-2 expression.
rows.discovery_query: ((berberine[Title/Abstract] OR inositol[Title/Abstract] OR chromium[Title/Abstract] OR "alpha-lipoic acid"[Title/Abstract] OR probiotic[Title/Abstract]) AND (glucose[Title/Abstract] OR insulin[Title/Abstract] OR "metabolic syndrome"[Title/Abstract] OR PCOS[Title/Abstract] OR obesity[Title/Abstract])) AND 2018:2026[pdat] AND hasabstract[text]
rows.abstract: Berberine (BBR), a plant-derived isoquinoline alkaloid, has been reported to exert anti-hyperglycemic and renoprotective effects. However, the mechanism by which BBR regulates renal glucose transport under diabetic conditions remains unclear. Sodium-glucose cotransporter-2 (SGLT-2), mainly expressed in renal proximal tubular epithelial cells, plays a key role in renal glucose reabsorption. This study investigated whether BBR attenuates diabetic kidney injury by regulating SGLT-2 expression and examined the potential involvement of FOXO1 and SP1 in this regulation. Db/db mice and high-glucose-exposed human kidney-2 (HK-2) cells were used to evaluate the effects of BBR, empagliflozin (EM), and their combination. Metabolic and renal phenotypes were assessed by biochemical, histological, and ultrastructural analyses. Network pharmacology, public transcriptomic data mining, molecular docking, cellular thermal shift assay (CETSA), quantitative real-time PCR, western blotting, immunofluorescence, nuclear-cytoplasmic fractionation, co-immunoprecipitation, 2-NBDG uptake, dual-luciferase reporter assays, FOXO1 overexpression, and pharmacological interference with SP1-associated regulation were performed to investigate the regulatory mechanism. Both BBR and EM improved metabolic abnormalities and renal injury in db/db mice, whereas combined treatment produced marked metabolic and renal improvements but was accompanied by an increasing trend in AST. BBR reduced hyperglycemia, improved glucose tolerance and enhanced the glucose-lowering response to exogenous insulin during the ITT, suppressed urinary albumin excretion, and alleviated renal histopathological and ultrastructural damage. Molecular docking and qualitative CETSA findings suggested that FOXO1 may represent a potential molecular target of BBR. In HK-2 cells, high-glucose stimulation increased SGLT-2 expression and glucose uptake, accompanied by dysregulation of FOXO1 and SP1 signaling. BBR downregulated FOXO1 and SGLT-2, restored SP1 and phosphorylated FOXO1 levels, and reduced glucose uptake under high-glucose conditions. FOXO1 overexpression attenuated the BBR-induced reduction in SGLT-2 expression, whereas pharmacological interference with SP1-associated regulation further supported the functional involvement of SP1 in SGLT-2 regulation. BBR attenuates diabetic kidney injury, at least in part, through FOXO1/SP1-associated regulation of renal SGLT-2 expression. These findings support the involvement of a FOXO1/SP1-associated regulatory axis in renal tubular glucose handling under diabetic conditions.
rows.verified_title: Berberine attenuates diabetic kidney injury via FOXO1/SP1-associated regulation of renal SGLT-2 expression.

rows.title: Vitamin D signaling in thymic development and longevity.
rows.discovery_query: (("vitamin D"[Title/Abstract] OR "vitamin B12"[Title/Abstract] OR folate[Title/Abstract] OR iron[Title/Abstract]) AND (fatigue[Title/Abstract] OR cognition[Title/Abstract] OR mood[Title/Abstract] OR deficiency[Title/Abstract] OR supplementation[Title/Abstract])) AND 2018:2026[pdat] AND hasabstract[text]
rows.abstract: Vitamin D has pleiotropic physiological roles including immune system regulation. Notably, there are links between vitamin D deficiency and risk of autoimmunity. Hormonal vitamin D binds to the vitamin D receptor (VDR) to exert its genomic effects. In immune cells, these include regulation of activation, inflammatory responses, and cytokine production. However, vitamin D supplementation is not efficacious in treatment of existing autoimmune disease. Conversely, vitamin D intake during childhood is associated with reduced risk of developing autoimmune type 1 diabetes. This supports a prophylactic role for vitamin D during this early developmental period wherein T cells undergo maturation in the thymus; importantly, highly self-reactive thymocytes undergo apoptosis due to interactions with specialized antigen presenting cells. Central to this process is the transcription factor autoimmune regulator (AIRE), which induces ectopic expression tissue restricted antigens in medullary thymic epithelial cells. Impaired AIRE function results in multiorgan autoimmunity in mice and humans. Vitamin D signaling regulates Aire expression and function in the mouse and, importantly, supports long-term thymic health by delaying aging-associated thymic involution. In humans, thymic aging is correlated with reduced naïve T cell output, impaired response to infection and cancer, and increased risk of autoimmunity. Collectively, existing data suggest that vitamin D sufficiency throughout the lifespan may be important for generating a self-tolerant T cell repertoire through its effects on AIRE and during aging by delaying aging-associated thymic involution. However, little is known about the links between thymic longevity and vitamin D status in humans, which represents a substantial knowledge gap.
rows.verified_title: Vitamin D signaling in thymic development and longevity.

rows.title: Association Between Digestive Power and Serum Vitamin B12 Levels in Young Adult Females: An Analytical Cross-Sectional Study.
rows.discovery_query: (("vitamin D"[Title/Abstract] OR "vitamin B12"[Title/Abstract] OR folate[Title/Abstract] OR iron[Title/Abstract]) AND (fatigue[Title/Abstract] OR cognition[Title/Abstract] OR mood[Title/Abstract] OR deficiency[Title/Abstract] OR supplementation[Title/Abstract])) AND 2018:2026[pdat] AND hasabstract[text]
rows.abstract: Digestive power (Agni) is a fundamental Ayurvedic concept that governs digestion and metabolism. Vitamin B12 is an essential micronutrient required for red blood cell formation, neurological function, and DNA synthesis. However, scientific evidence evaluating the relationship between digestive power and vitamin B12 levels remains limited. This study aimed to determine the association between digestive power and serum vitamin B12 levels among females aged 19-28 years using a laboratory immunoassay method. Materials and methods: A cross-sectional analytical study was carried out among 94 young adult females, including 47 vitamin B12-deficient and 47 vitamin B12-nondeficient females aged 19-28 years, selected through convenience sampling. Serum vitamin B12 was estimated using a standard laboratory immunoassay method, and participants were classified into four categories based on digestive strength (Agnibala) using a validated assessment tool. Data were analyzed using descriptive statistics, Pearson's chi-square test, independent Student's t-test, and multiple linear regression. A p-value ≤ 0.05 was considered statistically significant. Results: Serum vitamin B12 levels differed significantly between the deficient and nondeficient groups (p < 0.001). Balanced digestive power (Samagni) was predominantly observed among vitamin B12-nondeficient participants. In contrast, irregular digestive power (Vishamagni), elevated digestive power (Tikshnagni), and subdued digestive power (Mandagni) were more common among vitamin B12-deficient participants. The distribution of digestive power was significantly associated with vitamin B12 status, as demonstrated by Pearson's Chi-square test (χ² = 23.16, df = 3, p < 0.001). Conclusion: Digestive power showed a significant association with serum vitamin B12 levels. Balanced digestive power was predominantly observed in individuals with normal vitamin B12 levels, whereas disturbed digestive power was relatively higher in deficient participants. These findings suggest that digestive metabolic efficiency may be associated with micronutrient assimilation and warrant further prospective studies.
rows.verified_title: Association Between Digestive Power and Serum Vitamin B12 Levels in Young Adult Females: An Analytical Cross-Sectional Study.

rows.title: Mitochondrial-targeted DNA nanostructures deliver NAD(+) to attenuate mitochondrial oxidative injury in renal ischemia-reperfusion.
rows.discovery_query: ((riboflavin[Title/Abstract] OR nicotinamide[Title/Abstract] OR "alpha-lipoic acid"[Title/Abstract]) AND (mitochondrial[Title/Abstract] OR fatigue[Title/Abstract] OR energy[Title/Abstract] OR exercise[Title/Abstract])) AND 2015:2026[pdat] AND hasabstract[text]
rows.abstract: Renal ischemia-reperfusion injury (IRI) is a leading cause of acute kidney injury (AKI) and is associated with substantial morbidity, delayed recovery, and impaired quality of life. Its progression is closely linked to mitochondrial oxidative stress, nicotinamide adenine dinucleotide (NAD+) depletion, and insufficient tubular repair. NAD+ is a key cofactor that sustains mitochondrial bioenergetics and redox homeostasis and supports sirtuin-dependent repair signaling. Therefore, restoring NAD+ metabolism is an attractive therapeutic strategy for IRI. Nevertheless, direct NAD+ administration is limited by poor membrane permeability, rapid metabolic turnover, and insufficient tissue exposure. Tetrahedral DNA nanostructures (TDNs), as programmable and biocompatible DNA nanomaterials, provide an attractive platform for precision drug delivery and chemical functionalization. Here, we constructed TDN-TPP@NAD+, a triphenylphosphonium (TPP)-functionalized TDN carried NAD+ to improve its delivery context in renal IRI. TDN-TPP@NAD+ promoted intracellular delivery of NAD+ in hypoxia-injured HK-2 cells and sustained renal retention after systemic administration. The delivered NAD+ alleviated mitochondrial damage and was associated with restoration of SIRT1-PGC1α-mtTFA signaling, while the TDN scaffold also contributed to the reduction of excessive ROS through its intrinsic antioxidant properties. Thus TDN-TPP@NAD+ reduced tubular pathological injury, and improved renal biochemical indices in vivo. TDN-TPP@NAD+ provides a promising nanotherapeutic strategy for IRI-induced AKI and mitochondrial metabolic disorder-related diseases.
rows.verified_title: Mitochondrial-targeted DNA nanostructures deliver NAD+ to attenuate mitochondrial oxidative injury in renal ischemia-reperfusion.

rows.title: Fermented Polygonatum kingianum polysaccharide exerts enhanced anti-obesity effects by modulating the gut microbiota-GDCA-TGR5 axis.
rows.journal: Phytomedicine : international journal of phytotherapy and phytopharmacology
rows.discovery_query: ((berberine[Title/Abstract] OR inositol[Title/Abstract] OR chromium[Title/Abstract] OR "alpha-lipoic acid"[Title/Abstract] OR probiotic[Title/Abstract]) AND (glucose[Title/Abstract] OR insulin[Title/Abstract] OR "metabolic syndrome"[Title/Abstract] OR PCOS[Title/Abstract] OR obesity[Title/Abstract])) AND 2018:2026[pdat] AND hasabstract[text]
rows.abstract: Probiotic-fermented Polygonatum kingianum polysaccharide (FPKP0) was previously confirmed to exhibit enhanced anti-adipogenic activity in 3T3-L1 cells in vitro owing to altered structural, prompting an examination of whether this modified FPKP0 exerts superior anti-obesity effects in vivo via related mechanism in high-fat diet-fed mice. Physiological results showed that FPKP0 outperformed unfermented PKP0 accounting for reducing body weight, improving blood lipids, alongside alleviating hepatic steatosis and colonic damage. Correspondingly, FPKP0 reshaped the gut microbiota by boosting beneficial genera (especially Akkermansia muciniphila) and suppressing harmful bacteria (e.g., Dubosiella, Helicobacter). Integrated metagenomic and metabolomic analyses identified A. muciniphila and Glycodeoxycholic acid (GDCA) as the key microbial and metabolic factors with the in vivo effects of FPKP0. A strong positive correlation (ρ = 0.83) between A. muciniphila abundance and GDCA levels suggests a potential relationship between microbial remodeling and bile acid metabolism following FPKP0 intervention. Further mechanistic exploration suggested that TGR5 may serve as a downstream receptor associated with FPKP0-related changes in GDCA. Molecular docking and immunoblotting indicated a GDCA-TGR5 interaction and activation of the Gsα-PKA-CREB-UCP1 cascade to stimulate energy expenditure. This enhanced in vivo anti-obesity effect of FPKP0 may involve modulation of the gut microbiota (AKK)-bile acid (GDCA)-TGR5 axis, supporting the potential of FPKP0 as a functional food additive to combat obesity and related disorders.
rows.verified_title: Fermented Polygonatum kingianum polysaccharide exerts enhanced anti-obesity effects by modulating the gut microbiota-GDCA-TGR5 axis.

rows.title: Application of Cu(2+)-chelated curcumin/chitosan coating in maintaining the storage quality of harvested passion fruit.
rows.discovery_query: ((ashwagandha[Title/Abstract] OR rhodiola[Title/Abstract] OR ginseng[Title/Abstract] OR bacopa[Title/Abstract] OR "Hericium erinaceus"[Title/Abstract] OR curcumin[Title/Abstract] OR Ganoderma[Title/Abstract]) AND (sleep[Title/Abstract] OR stress[Title/Abstract] OR anxiety[Title/Abstract] OR cognition[Title/Abstract] OR fatigue[Title/Abstract] OR metabolic[Title/Abstract] OR safety[Title/Abstract])) AND 2018:2026[pdat] AND hasabstract[text]
rows.abstract: Passion fruit is susceptible to postharvest spoilage, requiring innovative preservation strategies. This study developed a novel Cu2+-chelated curcumin/chitosan composite coating (CuCur-CS) via self-assembly. Under ambient temperature, CuCur-CS treatment was the most effective, exhibiting the lowest weight loss rate (only 5.6% on day 18), along with superior fruit shape and surface color retention. The coating stabilized sugar-acid balance by suppressing respiration and alleviating oxidative stress. By day 18, H2O2 and MDA contents in the control increased by 53% and 28%, respectively, versus only 11% and 12% in CuCur-CS. Metabolomics revealed that CuCur-CS attenuated energy metabolism by stabilizing TCA cycle intermediates, while modulating phenylpropanoid and fatty acid pathways to suppress volatile alcohols, esters, and excessive phenolics and flavonoids. These actions delay aroma degradation and prevent antioxidant overactivation. Overall, CuCur-CS effectively retards senescence and postharvest losses, offering a promising preservation solution for passion fruit.
rows.verified_title: Application of Cu2+-chelated curcumin/chitosan coating in maintaining the storage quality of harvested passion fruit.

rows.title: Curcumin attenuates chronic heat stress-induced cardiac injury in Siberian sturgeon (Acipenser baerii): Mechanisms of oxidative stress, mitochondrial dysfunction and metabolic reprogramming.
rows.journal: Comparative biochemistry and physiology. Part D, Genomics & proteomics
rows.discovery_query: ((ashwagandha[Title/Abstract] OR rhodiola[Title/Abstract] OR ginseng[Title/Abstract] OR bacopa[Title/Abstract] OR "Hericium erinaceus"[Title/Abstract] OR curcumin[Title/Abstract] OR Ganoderma[Title/Abstract]) AND (sleep[Title/Abstract] OR stress[Title/Abstract] OR anxiety[Title/Abstract] OR cognition[Title/Abstract] OR fatigue[Title/Abstract] OR metabolic[Title/Abstract] OR safety[Title/Abstract])) AND 2018:2026[pdat] AND hasabstract[text]
rows.abstract: Global warming increasingly threatens cold-water aquaculture, yet nutritional strategies for protecting the fish heart from chronic heat stress remain insufficiently understood. This study evaluated the protective effects of dietary curcumin against chronic heat stress (28 °C) in the hearts of Siberian sturgeon (Acipenser baerii) using histological, biochemical, molecular, and metabolomic analyses. Heat stress caused cardiac injury, as indicated by inflammatory infiltration, mitochondrial vacuolization, increased serum cardiac enzymes (CK, CK-MB, and α-HBDH) and glucose, and elevated myocardial reactive oxygen species (ROS), superoxide dismutase (SOD) activity, and malondialdehyde (MDA) content. Curcumin supplementation attenuated these alterations and enhanced catalase (CAT) and glutathione peroxidase (GSH-Px) activities. Curcumin also reduced cardiomyocyte apoptosis by downregulating caspase-3, caspase-7, and caspase-9 and restoring heat shock protein 90 (Hsp90) levels. In addition, curcumin improved mitochondrial membrane potential (MMP), Ca2+/Mg2+-ATPase activity, and ATP content. Metabolomic profiling indicated that heat stress altered energy-related metabolites such as ATP and isocitrate, whereas curcumin partially restored the metabolic profile, most notably ATP. These findings support dietary curcumin as a practical nutritional strategy for improving cardiac protection and thermal resilience in Siberian sturgeon aquaculture.
rows.verified_title: Curcumin attenuates chronic heat stress-induced cardiac injury in Siberian sturgeon (Acipenser baerii): Mechanisms of oxidative stress, mitochondrial dysfunction and metabolic reprogramming.
rows.verified_journal: Comparative biochemistry and physiology. Part D, Genomics & proteomics

rows.title: Emerging Role of Natural Products and Dietary Supplements in Major Depressive Disorder: Therapeutic and Mechanistic Insights.
rows.discovery_query: ((saffron[Title/Abstract] OR omega-3[Title/Abstract] OR EPA[Title/Abstract] OR magnesium[Title/Abstract]) AND (depression[Title/Abstract] OR depressive symptoms[Title/Abstract] OR mood[Title/Abstract])) AND 2015:2026[pdat] AND hasabstract[text]
rows.abstract: Major Depressive Disorder (MDD) is the fourth highest cause of morbidity and mortality in the world, and its prevalence has grown significantly during the COVID-19 pandemic. The pathophysiology of the disorder is multifactorial, involving genetic, environmental, cellular, and molecular factors. Traditional pharmacotherapies are characterized by delayed action, inadequate response, and side effects, thus prompting studies of complementary or additional treatments. The review aims to provide a comprehensive evaluation of the therapeutic potential of natural products and dietary supplements in MDD, clarify their mechanism of action, and identify new and integrative approaches to treatment. A systematic search was conducted through July 2025 across various databases, including PubMed, Google Scholar, Web of Science, repositories of traditional integrated resources, local dissertations, and monographs. The key terms included major depressive disorder with a combination of phytomedicine, natural products, dietary supplements, phytoconstituents, therapeutic potential, and mechanisms of action. The use of natural products and dietary supplements has emerged as a potential means to effectively treat MDD due to their ability to regulate dysregulated biochemical processes and mechanisms. Natural compounds such as polyphenols, alkaloids, terpenoids, and essential fatty acids use a variety of cellular and molecular pathways to have an antidepressant effect, including augmenting neurotransmitter levels, modulating the hypothalamic-pituitary-adrenal axis, reducing neuroinflammation, and inhibiting oxidative damage. Dietary supplements also contribute to mood regulation by supporting neuronal integrity, modulating the gut-brain axis, and maintaining immune homeostasis. The overall evidence suggests that natural interventions can be used to supplement traditional pharmacotherapy and enhance treatment success. The review provides a framework for the cellular and molecular pathways underlying the antidepressant effects of various natural compounds and dietary supplements, therefore establishing a foundation for future investigation and clinical use.
rows.verified_title: Emerging Role of Natural Products and Dietary Supplements in Major Depressive Disorder: Therapeutic and Mechanistic Insights.

rows.title: Molecular Footprints of Diabetic Peripheral Neuropathy: Investigating Transcriptional Modulation of Sphingolipid Metabolism, Myelin-specific Genes and Neurotrophic Factors Under Elevated Glucose and Harnessing Therapeutic Potential of DHA and ALA.
rows.discovery_query: ((berberine[Title/Abstract] OR inositol[Title/Abstract] OR chromium[Title/Abstract] OR "alpha-lipoic acid"[Title/Abstract] OR probiotic[Title/Abstract]) AND (glucose[Title/Abstract] OR insulin[Title/Abstract] OR "metabolic syndrome"[Title/Abstract] OR PCOS[Title/Abstract] OR obesity[Title/Abstract])) AND 2018:2026[pdat] AND hasabstract[text]
rows.abstract: Research has shown that disturbances in sphingolipid metabolic homeostasis are significant contributors to Diabetic Peripheral Neuropathy (DPN). Ceramides and their metabolites are cell signaling molecules involved in islet cell function, insulin resistance, β-cell apoptosis, and neurodegeneration. However, diabetes-related abnormalities in sphingolipid metabolism in peripheral nerves have received little attention in the scientific literature. Neuroblastoma cells (Neuro2a) were exposed to high glucose (50 mM). Alpha-lipoic acid (ALA; 50 μM) and docosahexaenoic acid (DHA; 50 μM) were considered therapeutic interventions. Myelin-specific and neurotrophin gene expression was also studied in Schwann cells (IMS32) and in DPN induced in mice with streptozotocin (150 mg/kg). High glucose reduced cell viability, compromised membrane integrity, and induced apoptosis, as revealed by MTT, propidium iodide, and Annexin V/PI assays. RT-qPCR analysis showed significantly higher mRNA levels of genes that regulate the de novo, salvage, and sphingomyelinase pathways. Bioactive sphingolipids (ceramide, sphingosine, ceramide-1-P, and sphingosine-1-P) were found elevated by ELISA. The apoptotic (AIF, Bak, Bax, Cas-3, Cas-9, and p53) and inflammatory (IL-6, IL-1β, TNF-α, iNOS, and NF-κB) genes were upregulated, while Bcl-2 was downregulated. mRNA expression of myelin-specific proteins and neurotrophic factors was also reduced in the sciatic nerves of DPN mice and HG-treated IMS32 cells. DHA and ALA were found to normalize nearly all anomalies induced by hyperglycemia. The genes regulating the de novo, salvage, and sphingomyelinase pathways were differentially modulated in diabetic conditions. We suggest that targeting those genes would be a safer approach to ameliorate ceramide-mediated nerve damage in diabetes. Myelin-specific genes, including NT-3, NT-4, NGF-β, BDNF, CNTF, and GDNF, were downregulated in the sciatic nerve of neuropathic animals. Treatment with ALA and DHA proved beneficial in reversing the conditions; hence, supplementation with ALA and DHA, in addition to the standard anti-diabetic treatment regimen, is suggested. These findings suggest significant implications of hyperglycemia on sphingolipid metabolic impairment, which, in turn, impacts cell integrity and viability, myelin stability, and neurodegeneration.
rows.verified_title: Molecular Footprints of Diabetic Peripheral Neuropathy: Investigating Transcriptional Modulation of Sphingolipid Metabolism, Myelin-specific Genes and Neurotrophic Factors Under Elevated Glucose and Harnessing Therapeutic Potential of DHA and ALA.

rows.title: A coupled iron-hypoxia selection model for the evolution of endometriosis-associated ovarian clear cell carcinoma.
rows.discovery_query: (("vitamin D"[Title/Abstract] OR "vitamin B12"[Title/Abstract] OR folate[Title/Abstract] OR iron[Title/Abstract]) AND (fatigue[Title/Abstract] OR cognition[Title/Abstract] OR mood[Title/Abstract] OR deficiency[Title/Abstract] OR supplementation[Title/Abstract])) AND 2018:2026[pdat] AND hasabstract[text]
rows.abstract: Ovarian clear cell carcinoma (OCCC) frequently arises in association with endometriosis and is characterized by iron-rich oxidative stress, hypoxia-responsive metabolic reprogramming, glycogen accumulation, and alterations in ferroptosis-regulatory pathways. Interactions among hypoxia, iron metabolism, oxidative stress, and ferroptosis are increasingly recognized, but their role during precursor evolution remains uncertain. We propose that chronic iron-rich oxidative stress and a hypoxic microenvironment may jointly alter the relative fitness of epithelial cells during the endometriosis-to-OCCC transition. Repeated exposure may create a putative ferroptosis-related selection filter that preferentially removes susceptible cells while enriching less-susceptible cellular subpopulations capable of sustained survival. Here, ferroptosis tolerance denotes relative survival under chronic or sublethal ferroptosis-related stress and does not imply experimentally demonstrated resistance; broader oxidative-stress adaptation alone is insufficient to establish it. Surviving populations may acquire an adaptive iron-handling state that constrains the metabolically available labile iron pool despite an iron-rich extracellular environment through changes in iron uptake, ferritin-mediated sequestration and turnover, mitochondrial utilization, cellular export, or extracellular-vesicle-mediated ferritin disposal. These mechanisms may cooperate with HIF-1α/SLC1A1-associated adaptation and NRF2/SLC7A11/GPX4/glutathione pathways. Loss-of-function alteration of ARID1A may contribute to oncogenic evolution, while ARID1A deficiency may also modify redox and ferroptotic vulnerability and thereby the intensity of selection. The novelty of this framework lies not in any single molecular interaction, but in applying interconnected iron, hypoxia, redox, and ferroptosis biology to an evolutionary selection model across the endometriosis-atypical endometriosis-OCCC continuum. The model predicts coordinated stress and iron-handling adaptations in precursor lesions, reproducible changes in population composition after repeated sublethal iron-hypoxia exposure, and, as a distinct outcome, durable phenotypic adaptation after washout. These predictions can be tested through cyst-fluid analysis, spatial profiling, and repeated-exposure, washout, rechallenge, and lineage-tracing experiments. The framework is a falsifiable hypothesis that may be supported, narrowed, reformulated, or rejected experimentally.
rows.verified_title: A coupled iron-hypoxia selection model for the evolution of endometriosis-associated ovarian clear cell carcinoma.
